---
title: "Key decision points"
date-modified: "2026-05-12"
---

The adoption of alternative data sources involves a sequence of related
decisions that shape both the technical and organisational direction of
implementation.

These decisions are rarely one-off and may need to be revisited as
experience grows, systems evolve, and data availability changes. Making
these decision points explicit can help NSOs plan their work more
coherently and avoid misalignment between strategy, methods, and
resources.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# What data to use, and for what purpose {#Keydecisionpoints-Whatdatatouseandforwhatpurpose end="1026" data-start="988"}

One of the first decisions concerns which data sources to use, and what
role they are expected to play in CPI production and other official
statistical outputs. Alternative data may be used to:

- Replace existing survey-based price collection

- Supplement existing sources to improve coverage or timeliness

- Support research and experimental indices prior to full production use

- Support other statistical outputs produced by an NSO

NSOs may also choose to adopt different data sources for different
product groups, depending on market structure, data availability, and
quality considerations.

When acquiring alternative data sources, NSOs may also wish to consider
whether the data could support statistical uses beyond CPI, such as
national accounts or purchasing power parities. For example, decisions
around the treatment of VAT, the definition of turnover, and the level
of aggregation may affect the suitability of the data for other
purposes. While CPI specific requirements will often take precedence,
early consideration of potential reuse may reduce duplication of data
acquisition and processing effort across the organisation. See
section [Other uses of alternative data
sources](other-uses-of-alternative-data-within-cpi.qmd).

Clarifying the purpose can help determine the level of methodological
ambition, the acceptable level of operational risk, and the extent to
which existing production processes may need to change.

# Sampling from the data versus using the full universe {#Keydecisionpoints-Samplingfromthedataversususingthefulluniverse end="1613" data-start="1556"}

Alternative data sources often provide far more observations than
traditional surveys, leading to a key decision on whether to work with
the full universe of observed prices or transactions, or whether to
construct samples from the data. Sampling approaches may reduce
processing burden, simplify quality assurance, and align more closely
with existing CPI practices. By contrast, using the full universe of
data may better capture product turnover and changes in consumption
patterns, but typically requires more advanced systems and methods.

This decision has direct implications for index method choice, system
design, and validation strategies, and should therefore be considered
alongside broader implementation plans. Sampling approaches are
discussed further in the section [Product sampling for price index
calculation](product-sampling-for-price-index-calculation.qmd).

# Choice of index method and compilation approach {#Keydecisionpoints-Choiceofindexmethodandcompilationapproach end="2999" data-start="2948"}

Index method selection is a central decision point and depends on
several interrelated factors, including data availability, product
churn, and revision policies. The choice between bilateral and
multilateral methods, as well as between static and dynamic compilation
approaches, should be informed by both data properties and
organisational constraints.

Where alternative data include quantity or expenditure information, NSOs
must decide whether and how this information will be used in index
compilation. This involves assessing the reliability and conceptual
suitability of the data, considering whether proxy measures are
appropriate where quantities are unavailable, and determining how
frequently weights should be updated.

These decisions strongly influence whether weighted or unweighted index
methods are feasible and affect how closely resulting indices reflect
consumer behaviour at detailed levels.

Many NSOs adopt a phased approach, beginning with simpler bilateral
methods and transitioning to multilateral approaches as experience and
system capability increase. Details of these methods are provided in the
section on [Price index methods](price-index-methods.qmd).

# Integration with existing production systems and user communication {#Keydecisionpoints-Integrationwithexistingproductionsystemsandusercommunication end="3740" data-start="3692"}

Alternative data sources rarely operate in isolation. NSOs must decide
how new data will be integrated with existing CPI production systems,
including traditional price surveys, aggregation structures, and
dissemination practices. In some cases, parallel systems may be
maintained during transition periods; in others, production processes
may be redesigned more fundamentally. See section [CPI production system
requirements](cpi-production-system-requirements.qmd) for
more information.

These decisions affect not only technical implementation but also
staffing, maintenance, and long-term sustainability.

Introducing alternative data sources may also affect CPI outputs, even
when headline results remain broadly similar. NSOs should therefore
consider how methodological changes will be tested and evaluated, how
impacts will be analysed, and how developments will be communicated to
users. Clear documentation and transparent decision-making are essential
to maintaining trust in official statistics during periods of change.
These aspects are discussed further in the section on
[Implementation](implementation.qmd).
